splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in the calculation.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: The circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to judicially create such a doctrine to extend punishment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: The circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of Section 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars relitigating previously presented claims — when bringing successive collateral attacks under Section 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to Section 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims in Section 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive motions under Section 2255, in addition to the requirements of Section 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to Section 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that Section 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing under Section 2255, meaning they need only satisfy Section 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures such as ballot-receipt deadlines. The outcome affects whether election-rule challenges can be brought before elections or are funneled into post-election disputes.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate has Article III standing to challenge election rules before an election based on the competitive injury of facing an allegedly unlawful electoral framework.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate lacks Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election absent a concrete, particularized injury beyond generalized competitive concerns.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to the Sentencing Commission's (or agency's) interpretation when a criminal sentencing guideline or statute is ambiguous. This split has deepened after Kisor v. Wilkie narrowed Auer deference and Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference applies to ambiguous provisions even in the criminal sentencing context, and lenity does not override the deference framework.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This affects whether defendants can receive sentences below mandatory minimums and has led to wildly different outcomes depending on jurisdiction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is disqualifying from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as effectively meaning 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation of the guideline or impermissibly expands the text. This affects career-offender designations for many defendants with prior conspiracy convictions.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline under Stinson, and conspiracy and attempt qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is invalid — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, particularly after Kisor narrowed deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar reliance on such changes, while others permit courts to consider them, especially after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6). This affects many prisoners serving lengthy stacked sentences.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in attempting to allow it.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as one factor among others when evaluating extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled. Some circuits hold the broad language encompasses any state drug offense, while others require a federal-law nexus. This matters for career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, because the Guidelines refer broadly to 'state law' offenses.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls — substance must be federally listed
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction does not qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' unless the substance at issue is also listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This affects debtors who experience property value increases during their bankruptcy proceedings.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under 11 U.S.C. § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the structure and legislative history of § 348(f)(1)(A), which was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must challenge conditions of confinement (including BOP decisions about prerelease custody under the First Step Act) through habeas corpus or may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to the terms and conditions of federal confinement — as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement — must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus or may proceed as civil rights or APA actions. This affects access to judicial review of BOP decisions on earned time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges affecting the duration of confinement, including BOP decisions on prerelease custody and earned time credits, must be brought through habeas corpus and not through civil rights or APA actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that conditions-of-confinement claims may be brought through civil rights statutes or the APA, and habeas is not the exclusive remedy for challenges that do not directly contest the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation sentencing, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows district courts to punish defendants for conduct violating supervised release, placing it at odds with other circuits that view revocation sentencing as addressing only the breach of trust, not as additional punishment for new criminal conduct. This affects hundreds of supervised release revocations per year.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants at revocation for the conduct that violated the conditions of supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation addresses breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentencing should be based on the defendant's breach of the court's trust inherent in the conditions of supervised release, not as punishment for the underlying violating conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees — filed in a criminal case but civil in nature — triggers the 30-day civil appeal deadline or the 14-day criminal appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but a minority takes the opposite position.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and therefore the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion is filed on the criminal docket, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are divided on whether compassionate release motions may encompass claims that overlap with habeas corpus relief — such as legal errors at trial or sentencing — or whether such claims must be channeled exclusively through § 2255. This affects prisoners who may lack an avenue for habeas relief but have potentially meritorious claims of legal error.

positions.label: May consider legal errors in compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider claims of legal error or unfairness in the original conviction or sentence as factors in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: May not consider legal errors in compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the validity of a conviction or sentence must be brought through § 2255 and cannot serve as the basis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
